task_title: Elements of Effective Teaching that Include Risk Management and Accident Prevention
objective: By the end of this lesson you can teach a learner to identify, assess and mitigate risk with PAVE, the risk matrix, TEAM and FRATs, fit that teaching to each phase of training, and manage the special risks of giving flight instruction, including hazardous attitudes, lost situational awareness and the takeoff and landing phases, while you model the safety habits you want the learner to copy.
why: Many accidents involve poor risk management decisions, so the FAA calls risk management one of the most important skills a pilot can learn and practice as a habit [[25:185|AIH 10-1]]. As the instructor you carry two jobs at once: teaching risk management and managing the extra risks of instruction itself, such as a learner flying a maneuver badly close to the ground [[25:185|AIH 10-1]] [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. On the CFI checkride you will be asked to teach these tools and to show them in the airplane.

prereading.label: AIH 10-1 to 10-9
prereading.what: Chapter 10, Teaching Practical Risk Management during Flight Instruction. The core of this Task: when to teach it, tools, teaching by phase, instruction risks, best practices, takeoffs and landings.

prereading.label: AIH 1-1 to 1-14
prereading.what: Risk management principles and process, PAVE, IMSAFE, the risk matrix, FRATs, 3P, situational awareness and its obstacles.

prereading.label: AIH 1-15 to 1-28
prereading.what: SRM and the 5 Ps, ADM and the error chain, hazardous attitudes, stress, resources, workload, teaching and assessing decision-making.

prereading.label: RMH 3-1 to 3-11
prereading.what: Hazards and risk, hazardous attitudes, leading accident causes, PAVE in detail, numerical and narrative FRATs.

prereading.label: RMH 4-1 to 5-5
prereading.what: Assessing risk with the matrix and its errors, then mitigating it. Follow Tricia's case study all the way through.

prereading.label: PHAK 2-1 to 2-25
prereading.what: ADM, CRM and SRM, the 5 Ps, 3P with PAVE, CARE and TEAM, DECIDE, operational pitfalls, situational awareness and workload.

prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-11
prereading.what: Positive exchange of flight controls, the sterile flight deck and see and avoid.

warmup: Think first: your pre-solo learner shows up 20 minutes late, says work was awful, and asks if you can "just do stalls quickly" because the ceiling is coming down. Which of her words are hazards? Who should decide whether you fly, and how would you get her to make that call herself instead of you making it for her?

key_terms.def: A present condition, event, object or circumstance that could lead to or contribute to an accident, such as a nick in the propeller [[25:7|AIH 1-3]].

The future impact of a hazard that is not controlled or eliminated, measured by exposure, severity and probability [[25:7|AIH 1-3]]. The RMH calls it the composite of severity and likelihood [[30:19|RMH 3-1]].
A decision-making process to identify hazards systematically, assess the degree of risk and determine the best course of action [[25:7|AIH 1-3]].
A checklist that sorts hazards into four buckets: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment and External pressures [[25:8|AIH 1-4]] [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

A table that crosses likelihood (probable, occasional, remote, improbable) with severity (catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible) to give a composite risk level [[30:34|RMH 4-1]] [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].
Flight Risk Assessment Tool: a form for recording each hazard and its risk during flight planning. It can be numerical or narrative [[30:28|RMH 3-10]] [[30:29|RMH 3-11]].
The mitigation choices: Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate [[25:188|AIH 10-4]] [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]].
Aeronautical decision-making: a systematic approach to the mental process pilots use to consistently find the best course of action for a set of circumstances [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].
Single-pilot resource management: the art and science of managing all resources on board and outside the aircraft available to a single pilot [[25:19|AIH 1-15]].
Crew resource management: training focused on effective use of all resources (people, hardware and information) to help a crew cooperate and decide well [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]].
Accurate perception and understanding of all factors within the risk elements that affect safety before, during and after the flight [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].
Five attitudes that hurt decisions: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability, macho and resignation [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

body.p: Start with the words, because learners mix them up. A hazard is a present condition that could lead to an accident; risk is the future impact of that hazard if it is not controlled; safety is a relative term, because complete freedom from hazards is not possible [[25:7|AIH 1-3]]. The RMH uses the street-crossing picture: traffic is always a hazard, but the risk only becomes significant when you step into the street [[30:19|RMH 3-1]].

The process has three steps, applied in order: identify the hazard, assess the risk, mitigate the risk [[25:7|AIH 1-3]] [[25:8|AIH 1-4]]. Each step is a building block for the next, and if identification is interrupted to fix one hazard, more important ones can be missed [[25:8|AIH 1-4]]. The four principles behind it are: accept no unnecessary risk, make risk decisions at the appropriate level, accept risk when benefits outweigh costs, and integrate risk management into planning at all levels [[25:7|AIH 1-3]].

head: Step
What the learner does
How you teach it
rows: Identify
Sorts hazards into the PAVE buckets and looks at every sub-element in each one [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]

Coach the learner to use PAVE methodically. Show that some hazards are almost always red, such as a solid line of thunderstorms ahead or IMC before takeoff for a pilot or airplane not equipped and current for IFR [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]
Assess
Rates likelihood and severity, then reads the composite risk from the matrix [[30:34|RMH 4-1]] [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]

Lead the learner through assessment at first. Use an event with a low but fairly fixed likelihood, such as an engine failure after takeoff, and have the learner work out the outcomes of different responses to find the severity [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]
Mitigate
Picks TEAM actions: transfer, eliminate, accept or mitigate, then consciously accepts what is left [[25:187|AIH 10-3]] [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]

Teach that mitigation can start days or weeks before a flight, like buying an airline ticket when widespread icing is forecast (transfer) or cancelling a recreational flight (eliminate) [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]

body.p: Mitigate every high (red) and serious (yellow) risk. Medium (green) risks may also be mitigated when possible, following the principle of accepting no unnecessary risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Red or yellow means no-go unless a new assessment after mitigation shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

The last step is deciding whether to accept the remaining risk, done consciously and on behalf of any passengers. In dual instruction you mitigate the risk of the learner's actions by operating at a safe altitude and guarding the controls, then you consciously accept what remains and stay vigilant [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

callout.text: Many learners already manage risk at work, even if the hazards are different. Acknowledge that expertise and involve them in the aviation risk decisions [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].
An unprepared learner is a serious hazard. A syllabus, quality ground instruction and a thorough briefing before each flight are themselves mitigation [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

check.q: A learner rates a runway overrun at a short strip as "occasional" likelihood and "critical" severity. What composite risk does the matrix give?
check.a: Serious (yellow), the same reading the RMH gives for its marginal-runway overrun example. It means no-go unless mitigation brings the next assessment to medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

body.p: Pilot/Aircraft/enVironment/External Pressures (PAVE) checklist. PAVE divides the risks of a flight into four categories and is used in all stages of flight planning [[25:8|AIH 1-4]]. The AIH calls its categories convenient buckets for risk identification [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

head: Letter
What to check
Teaching point
rows: P: Pilot
Qualification, currency and proficiency, plus aeromedical fitness (IMSAFE) [[25:187|AIH 10-3]] [[30:22|RMH 3-4]] [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
"P" applies to both the learner and the instructor [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Currency is legal; proficiency is whether you can manage the conditions [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]
A: Aircraft
Right airplane, equipped, runway and load capability, altitude performance, fuel with reserves [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]
Book performance comes from a new airplane flown by a test pilot, so build in margins [[25:9|AIH 1-5]]
V: enVironment
Weather, terrain, airports, airspace, night [[25:9|AIH 1-5]] [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]
Weather is the most variable environmental hazard [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]
E: External pressures
Someone waiting, a passenger you do not want to disappoint, "get-there-itis", pride [[25:10|AIH 1-6]]
The key category: it can make a pilot ignore all the others [[25:11|AIH 1-7]]

body.p: IMSAFE is the "P" tool for physical and mental readiness: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion [[25:11|AIH 1-7]] [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. The RMH notes some publications fold Emotion into Stress and use the E for Eating [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

Personal minimums turn PAVE into limits. A pilot with 10 knots of crosswind experience keeps 10 knots as a personal limit even if the AFM shows 15, until more training with an instructor [[25:8|AIH 1-4]]. Teach the difference between what is legal and what is smart [[25:9|AIH 1-5]].

External pressure tools you can hand the learner: allow time for an extra fuel stop, keep backup airline reservations, tell people waiting that you may be late, manage passenger expectations and carry an overnight kit [[25:11|AIH 1-7]].

callout.text: PAVE is for perceiving hazards, CARE (Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors) for processing them, and TEAM for performing the risk control. Together they make the 3P model [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

check.q: Why does the AIH call management of external pressure the single most important key to risk management?
check.a: Because it is the one category that can cause a pilot to ignore all the other risk factors, and it figures into a majority of accidents [[25:11|AIH 1-7]].

chunks.title: Flight risk assessment tools and other aids

body.p: Flight Risk Assessment Tools (FRATs). A FRAT is the form used to record each hazard and its risk during flight planning [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]. It enables proactive hazard identification and helps pilots tell a low-risk flight from a high-risk one in advance [[25:14|AIH 1-10]]. A formal pen-and-paper process helps because personal desires can bend an informal risk assessment [[25:14|AIH 1-10]].

head: Type
How it works
Watch out for
rows: Numerical FRAT
Each listed hazard carries a number; the total falls into a low, caution or danger range [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]
May miss hazards on this flight, ranges can look arbitrary, it does not make the pilot analyze each hazard, and a low total can hide one serious hazard [[30:29|RMH 3-11]]
Narrative FRAT
The pilot names each hazard by PAVE area, assigns likelihood and severity, then records a mitigation [[30:29|RMH 3-11]]
Takes longer, but fixes many weaknesses of the numerical form [[30:29|RMH 3-11]]

body.p: Thresholds. An effective FRAT has at least three score ranges, often green, yellow and red. If every flight scores acceptable under any condition, the thresholds are probably set wrong [[25:15|AIH 1-11]].

callout.text: Use numerical FRATs with caution. A line of embedded thunderstorms across the route may be the only item scored, so the total suggests "go" with no mitigation [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

body.p: Other tools in the kit: the TEAM acronym and the risk matrix are the primary tools for teaching risk management [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]. The 3P model (Perceive, Process, Perform) runs in parallel with identify, assess, mitigate and is a continuous loop [[25:16|AIH 1-12]]. The 5P check (Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers, Programming) is reviewed at set decision points in flight [[25:20|AIH 1-16]]. The FAA Personal Minimums Checklist in the AIH appendix reflects the PAVE approach [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].

Scale the tool to the flight. For a local flight, a short PAVE review is acceptable; for a longer or more complex flight, a FRAT may be worth completing [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]. The RMH agrees that a FRAT may not be necessary for a simple local flight on a calm sunny day [[30:42|RMH 5-4]].

check.q: Which kind of FRAT should a pre-solo learner meet first, and who shows it?
check.a: A non-numerical FRAT, demonstrated by the instructor during the first few flights [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

chunks.title: When and how to introduce risk management

body.p: When. Teach risk management at the very start of flight training and weave it into actual flight training rather than as a separate subject. It works even better if the learner gets ground instruction on it before the first flight lesson, and it belongs in any formal ground school [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. It is never too early: make the 3P discussion a standard part of the preflight discussion [[25:16|AIH 1-12]].

Where. Put risk management activity and discussion in every preflight and postflight briefing, and let learners lead those discussions as they gain experience [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]. The syllabus should include risk management unique to each stage, with risks that get more subtle as training goes on [[25:149|AIH 7-5]].
How. The AIH describes system safety training in three phases [[25:30|AIH 1-26]] [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]:

bullets: Phase I: stick-and-rudder skill first, so the learner is confident flying the airplane [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

Phase II: the hazards and considerations of that maneuver, much of it discussed on the ground with no added flight time, such as the same airplane on a 1,800-foot strip with an obstacle at high density altitude [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].
Phase III: a complex scenario that puts those hazards into a whole flight [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

body.p: Do not drop risk management after the first certificate. Recurrent training, transition training, flight reviews and instrument proficiency checks should include it too [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

callout.text: Introduce risk management by letting the learner make real but low-stakes calls: fitness to fly, the weather and equipment problems. When a discrepancy turns up on preflight, let the learner decide first, then discuss the options [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Risk management habits are built like any flying skill: through repetition and consistent use of specific procedures [[25:16|AIH 1-12]].

check.q: Your new learner signs up today. When should the first risk management instruction happen?
check.a: Before the first flight lesson, as ground instruction, then built into every flight and briefing from then on [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

chunks.title: Risk management teaching by phase of instruction

body.p: Use a building block approach. It works for new pilots and for experienced pilots who never had formal risk management training [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

head: Phase
What the learner should do
Your role
rows: Pre-solo
Be able to conduct a basic risk management analysis by the first solo [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Lead and guide. Brief risk on every flight and demonstrate a non-numerical FRAT on the first few flights [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Post-solo, before cross-country
Do the risk analysis of each planned flight with occasional coaching, and debrief you on the risk side of each solo [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Review the analysis for every solo flight and give feedback [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Cross-country
Do a full risk analysis, with a FRAT or another method, for every dual and solo cross-country [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Review and approve it like the rest of the preflight work [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Instrument
Analyze complex weather and other risk elements: single-engine IFR, single alternator or radio, night, low IMC, icing [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Emphasize broad strategies, because IMC hazards are high [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Transition
Handle more complex systems, avionics, performance and emergency procedures, or less performance in a lighter airplane [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Know the airplane yourself first; use scenarios in the NAS and stress automation, workload and situational awareness [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Recurrent, flight reviews, IPCs
Show risk management in scenarios that mirror their normal flying, plus any new kind of flying they plan [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Emphasize it; many pilots certificated before the ACS never had formal training in it [[25:189|AIH 10-5]]
Professional pilots
Adapt crew habits to single-pilot flying in their own airplanes [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Emphasize risk management in transition training [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]

body.p: For pilots already certificated, encourage risk management on every flight, scaled to its complexity, so it becomes intuitive: part of the preparation for every flight and continuous while it lasts [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

Grade decision skills progressively too. The AIH grades SRM as Explain, Practice and Manage/Decide [[25:32|AIH 1-28]], and suggests an area such as automation management might move from a describe item on flight one to practice by flight three and manage-decide by flight five [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: Flight review example from the AIH: a pilot who flies between rural Class E airports plans to start flying into Class B. Cover the operating requirements such as Mode C and ADS-B, and the environmental risks of Class B [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

check.q: At the end of each solo flight before cross-country training, what should the learner do?
check.a: Debrief the instructor on the risk management aspects of the flight [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

body.p: ADM is a systematic approach to the mental process pilots use to consistently pick the best course of action [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. System safety asks pilots to use ADM, risk management, situational awareness and SRM together, and these are often collectively called ADM [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. About 80 percent of aviation accidents are estimated to be human factors related [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. Good judgment can be taught; it is not just a by-product of experience [[1:42|PHAK 2-3]].

The error chain. Accidents are usually a chain of events, and breaking one link is usually enough to change the outcome. Teach it with real accident stories, like the AIH's 100-hour pilot who skipped the briefing, used a rule-of-thumb fuel figure, launched tired into building weather and ran short of fuel [[25:23|AIH 1-19]] [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

Decision models to teach: define the problem, choose a course of action, implement and evaluate [[25:24|AIH 1-20]] [[25:26|AIH 1-22]]; the DECIDE loop (Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate) [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]]; and 3P [[25:16|AIH 1-12]]. In emergencies with no time, experts use automatic or naturalistic decision-making, which improves with training and experience [[1:60|PHAK 2-21]].

head: CRM
SRM
rows: What it is
Effective use of all resources by a crew to cooperate and decide well [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]
Managing all resources on board and outside, before and during flight, by a single pilot [[25:19|AIH 1-15]]
When to use it
When the flight has more than one pilot: one flies the path, the other monitors, and both state reasoning, intentions and actions [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]
Most training airplanes and owner flying. ATC and Flight Service replicate CRM for the single pilot [[25:19|AIH 1-15]]
Teaching hook
Pilots from Part 142 training centers may already know CRM and threat and error management [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
The 5P check at preflight, pretakeoff, midpoint or hourly, predescent and before the FAF or pattern entry [[25:20|AIH 1-16]] [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]

body.p: Dual instruction is a small crew. You and the learner are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and the RMH notes a second pilot can be a flight instructor while warning that any extra person can also introduce threats [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

Resources and workload. Have learners name internal resources (their own knowledge, checklists, the POH, passengers) and external ones (ATC, Flight Service) [[25:28|AIH 1-24]] [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. When overloaded, the learner should stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

callout.text: Teach that declaring an emergency is an appropriate reaction: ATC gives priority, and 14 CFR 91.3 lets the PIC deviate from the rules as needed to meet an inflight emergency [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

check.q: Your learner flies with a friend who is also a pilot, and neither is named PIC. What SRM risk does the PHAK point out?
check.a: If no one is designated PIC and something unplanned happens, the decision-making styles of several self-confident pilots may conflict [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

chunks.title: Human behavior hazards and hazardous attitudes

body.p: Attitude is a motivational predisposition to respond to people, situations or events in a given way, and five attitudes are known to hurt sound decisions [[25:26|AIH 1-22]]. Recognizing a hazardous thought is the first step toward neutralizing it [[25:26|AIH 1-22]]. Then the pilot labels it hazardous and states the antidote, which should be memorized so it comes to mind automatically [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

Spot it and fix it right away. A learner who finds training easy may drift toward a hazardous attitude about their ability; point out the potential and teach the antidote [[25:27|AIH 1-23]]. Hazardous attitudes should be noticed immediately and corrected with the proper antidote [[25:27|AIH 1-23]].
Other human behavior hazards to manage:

bullets: Operational pitfalls such as peer pressure, mindset, get-there-itis, scud running, continuing VFR into IMC and getting behind the aircraft. Build them into your ADM scenarios [[25:18|AIH 1-14]] [[25:19|AIH 1-15]].

Stress. Performance rises with stress, peaks, then falls off fast. If a learner keeps cancelling in good weather, it may be worry about stalls, landings or solo; more explanation and encouragement may help [[25:27|AIH 1-23]] [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].
Expectation and confirmation bias: seeing what you expect, or explaining away information that does not fit. Fatigue makes both more likely [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].
Over-relying on yourself. The single pilot is their own quality control and tends to deny personal limits [[25:13|AIH 1-9]].

callout.text: Studies of accident-prone pilots found disdain for rules, thrill seeking, impulsiveness and under-use of outside sources such as instructors and ATC [[1:51|PHAK 2-12]]. If you see these traits, address them early.

check.q: A learner who finds training easy starts acting as if the checklist is beneath him. What does the AIH tell you to do?
check.a: Point out the potential for a hazardous attitude about his ability and teach the antidote, correcting it right away rather than letting it grow [[25:27|AIH 1-23]].

body.p: Hazards associated with providing flight instruction. The techniques are the same ones you teach, but a few hazards are unique to instruction [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Increase the scope of your risk management: it includes maneuvers flown incorrectly by the learner close to the ground [[25:185|AIH 10-1]], and the learner on the controls may be a significant hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Common flight instruction risks. The best way to analyze them is PAVE, and you should always do a risk analysis before giving instruction [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]:

head: Category
Common risk in instruction
rows: Pilot

The learner is generally less proficient than you. You may have your own currency, proficiency or aeromedical issues, and unfamiliarity with the airplane, avionics or procedures is a hazard. Expect the learner errors listed in the AFH [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Aircraft

A trainer you do not maintain may have inoperative equipment or overdue inspections you do not know about. Two-seat trainers often need less fuel to carry both of you, and performance may be marginal at high density altitude [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Environment

Crowded practice airspace, haze or pollution that hides traffic, complex airspace, full stalls that can become inadvertent spins, simulated engine failures that have caused real accidents, and practice approaches concentrating airplanes on one path [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
External pressures
Scheduling problems made worse by aircraft or weather problems, plus work, family and money pressures, causing distraction and anxiety that degrade performance [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]

body.p: The general mitigations: have the learner fly maneuvers only after appropriate training, pick practice areas with safe options, use sufficient altitude, stay alert for the unexpected from the learner or outside, and be ready to take over [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

callout.text: Do not create a hazard yourself by teaching at the wrong time or altitude, such as discussing takeoff technique while entering the runway, or teaching stalls below a cloud layer without room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Under PAVE, in which category does the AIH place the hazard of simulated engine failures done wrong?
check.a: Environmental risks, along with crowded airspace and inadvertent spins from full stalls [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Best practices for managing risk in instruction

body.p: Best practices. Always include the learner in risk management during dual instruction: you are both responsible for the lookout, and the learner helps resolve airworthiness status, airspace, NOTAMs and TFRs [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

head: Category
Best practice
rows: Pilot

Know the model and avionics before you teach in it, from reading the POH to flying it first. Monitor yourself with IMSAFE, and build enough trust that learners report their own aeromedical issues early so you can reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Aircraft

Check official airworthiness before the flight and before preflight, know the operator's discrepancy process, read the current discrepancy report and resolve questions with maintenance. Involve the learner [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Environment
Coach the learner through the assessment. In marginal VFR with stalls planned, discuss the risks and options: stay in the pattern, use a simulator, do ground school or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
External pressures
Ease schedule worries, offer to reschedule, switch to classroom work or end a lesson early if the learner seems worried about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]

body.p: Awareness and oversight of the learner's actions, with timely supervision, intervention or mitigation. Leave enough time and space for the learner to practice and for you to take over before things get beyond your ability to fly the airplane [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. On hazardous maneuvers and first attempts, be ready to take control at any time; when the learner is progressing, avoid unnecessary interruptions [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Never let a learner exceed your limits [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Awareness of the learner's cognitive and physiological state, with timely action against anxiety, fatigue or other obstructions to learning. Watch for fatigue, which may not show until serious errors are made [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. If a learner seems distracted or struggles, ask whether they were tired or uncomfortable, or whether something else in life is causing stress [[25:28|AIH 1-24]]. External pressures can cause anxiety that degrades performance [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

bullets: Identify hazards systematically and keep tracking them while maneuvering [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Discuss hazards and mitigations in detail before and after the flight [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].
Prompt the learner to find hazards and say their thinking out loud, such as collision hazards and a forced landing field before a ground reference maneuver [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

callout.text: Application: build the learner's IMSAFE check into your scheduling call the day before, so an honest "no" costs the learner nothing.

check.q: You are about to instruct in an airplane model with avionics you have never used. What range of preparation does the AIH describe?
check.a: Anything from reviewing the POH or avionics manuals to acquiring flight time in that equipment before giving instruction [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Special considerations: teaching takeoffs and landings

body.p: Special considerations while teaching takeoffs and landings. Most GA accidents happen in a small part of the flight: landing (24.1 percent) and takeoff (23.4 percent) [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]. The AIH margin-of-safety figure also shows the margin smallest in approach and landing, where a distraction can overtax the pilot [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

head: Phase
Risk
What you do
rows: Takeoff: when to teach
Takeoff takes seconds. The learner's attention is almost all on control, so words may not be heard, and talk can cause a missed tower call [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]

Teach airspeeds, pitch attitudes, references, control inputs and engine parameters before calling the tower or announcing on CTAF. It keeps the flight deck sterile and helps collision avoidance [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Takeoff: scenarios
A scenario can push the learner into an unsafe climb rate or pitch [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]

Use realistic takeoff scenarios, such as an imaginary obstacle at a realistic point. On soft-field takeoffs, watch drift in ground effect and do not let it grow beyond the learner's control [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Takeoff: spacing
Wake turbulence, poor in-trail spacing, conflict with landing traffic [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Make sure there is enough spacing before entering any runway space in use [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Landing: mechanical teaching
Teaching landings by rote leaves learners unable to handle changing conditions, leading to unstable approaches [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teach problems and solutions for the approach actually happening, and teach how to pick aiming and touchdown points for the airplane, landing type and conditions [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Landing: too much talk
Coaching on final reduces your lookout and situational awareness and causes missed radio calls [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Use only concise prompting on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Landing: unique risks
Unfamiliar fields, strong winds, slow short-field approach speeds, 180 degree power-off accuracy approaches [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teach pre-landing reconnaissance, have the skill for the wind yourself, guard slow-speed margins and anticipate the learner's errors [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]

callout.text: Learners may know not to sacrifice a stable approach for accuracy, yet still not be ready to apply it. Expect it on power-off accuracy approaches [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

check.q: What does the AIH say happens when an instructor teaches landings mechanically?
check.a: The learner is ill-equipped to identify or manage changing conditions, which can lead to unstable approaches and faulty landings [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

chunks.title: Keeping situational awareness while you teach

body.p: In flight you manage risk in real time by keeping situational awareness of the aircraft's state, traffic, weather, airspace and the surrounding area, and of what the learner is doing and plans to do [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. The RMH lists aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft, the environment and the human factors in play [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
Obstacles to maintaining situational awareness during flight instruction:

head: Obstacle
How it hurts
Defense
rows: Fatigue, stress, work overload
Fixation on one item instead of the whole flight [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Plan the workload; stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Distraction
A minor problem, like a gauge reading wrong, pulls attention from flying and scanning [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Fly the airplane first; in an emergency the first priority is to fly and keep a safe airspeed [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]
Complacency
Overconfidence from repetition, harder to spot than fatigue because all seems well; watch it in experienced pilots in familiar airplanes [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]
Crosscheck automation and position [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]
Your own teaching
Trying to convey a lot while also checking the airplane is flown safely cuts your lookout and awareness [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teach on the ground; brief concisely in the air [[25:192|AIH 10-8]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Programming
Avionics capture attention for long periods [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]
Plan when and where to program, and when not to [[25:22|AIH 1-18]]

body.p: Overall situational awareness of the aircraft's dynamic state, its position in space, and vigilance for unexpected events. Stay alert for the unexpected from the learner or from outside [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Continuous awareness of the aircraft's dynamic state and position in the NAS also means knowing the airspace and restrictions you are in, which in training areas may be complex [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and knowing why you are being vectored rather than just turning [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

To check the learner, ask about the positions of traffic in the pattern, engine indications and position on the chart, or focus them on an imaginary radio problem and see if they let flying or scanning slide [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

callout.text: Model "fly the airplane first" out loud: during a go-around, power, airspeed and configuration come before telling the tower [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

check.q: Name two quick in-flight checks the AIH suggests for testing whether a learner is keeping situational awareness.
check.a: Ask about traffic positions in the pattern, engine indications or the airplane's position on the chart, or focus the learner on an imaginary radio or navigation problem and see if flying or scanning slides [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

body.p: Learners treat the instructor as a role model and copy your habits, so your safety advice means little if you do not show it every time [[25:164|AIH 8-6]]. Demonstrate each skill exactly the way you want it practiced, including all safety procedures [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

head: Safety practice
What you model
What you teach
rows: Collision avoidance while simultaneously providing instruction
Keep scanning while you talk. If learners think you own the lookout, they never build the habit [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Both of you share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Clear before every turn and maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] and have the learner call "clear left, right, above, and below" [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Avoidance of unnecessary distractions
A sterile flight deck in critical phases: no nonessential activity, and modeled, not just taught [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Teach before the tower call and prompt concisely on final [[25:192|AIH 10-8]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Coordinated flight
Rudder in the direction of the turn in every demonstration [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Keep the ball centered and "step on the ball" [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Uncoordinated flight raises loss of control risk [[24:106|AFH 5-1]], and a spin needs a stall plus yaw [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]
Awareness of who is manipulating controls through positive exchange of flight controls
Brief the exchange before flight and use the three steps every time [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
The learner keeps flying until you say "I have the flight controls," with a visual check [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Continuous awareness of the aircraft's dynamic state and position in the NAS
Narrate your own awareness of the airplane, traffic, weather and airspace [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]
Ask the learner where traffic is and where you are on the chart [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]

body.p: Why the exchange matters: numerous accidents came from confusion over who had control, especially between learners and instructors [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. When you must take over, say "I have the flight controls" calmly and make sure the learner lets go; anxious learners can be very strong [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

Midair facts worth sharing: instructors were on board in 37 percent of the midair accidents studied, most happened in VFR daylight with good visibility, and most were at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Scanning is limited by blind spots and by time spent looking at instruments or tablets [[1:364|PHAK 14-30]].

check.q: Besides the three spoken steps, what does the AIH recommend during every control exchange?
check.a: A visual check that the other person actually has the flight controls, so there is never any doubt about who is flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: SBT for risk management and ADM

body.p: On the checkride the evaluator names a Task, and you use scenario-based training to demonstrate, teach and assess risk management and ADM inside it. SBT helps you teach ADM and risk management, and as soon as the learner starts deciding, you shift to mentor and facilitator [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].
A lesson flow you can use for almost any Task:

bullets: Ground: set the scenario, run PAVE out loud with the learner, rate the big risks on the matrix and pick TEAM actions [[25:187|AIH 10-3]] [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].
Brief: decide in advance which outcomes are good or poor, and give the learner freedom to decide, but never to act unsafely [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].
Air: introduce simulated hazards and ask the learner to identify, assess and mitigate them [[25:187|AIH 10-3]]. Prompt the learner to verbalize [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

Debrief: learner self-assessment first, then yours, then compare (collaborative assessment) [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Ask how the decision was reached, what resources were used and whether risk was assessed accurately [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

head: SRM grade
What the learner shows
rows: Explain
Can identify and describe the risks but has to be prompted [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Practice
Applies SRM in flight; your coaching fixes minor errors; an active decision maker [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Manage/Decide
Gathers the key data, weighs options and their risk, decides, and needs no instructor intervention [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Not observed
Event not done or not required [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]

callout.text: Example from the AIH: the tower offers a tailwind runway to expedite traffic. Have the learner assess the risks and propose alternatives [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

check.q: In an SBT flight, what happens to your role once the learner begins making decisions?
check.a: You keep demonstrating and instructing skill maneuvers, but you revert to the role of mentor and learning facilitator, turning planning and execution over to the learner as soon as possible [[25:31|AIH 1-27]].

body.p: These are instructor errors the sources warn about.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Teaching risk management as a separate lecture
A learner who can recite PAVE but never uses it [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]
Integrate it into every flight and briefing [[25:186|AIH 10-2]]
Trusting a low numerical FRAT score
A "go" with one extreme hazard unmitigated [[25:188|AIH 10-4]]
Look at each hazard; use PAVE or a narrative FRAT [[30:29|RMH 3-11]]
Making every go/no-go decision yourself
A learner who never practices the decision [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Have the learner assess the weather and make the call; the final choice is still yours [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]
Teaching at the wrong time or place
Talk on the runway, stalls under a cloud deck [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Teach on the ground; pick altitude and area with safe options [[25:190|AIH 10-6]] [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Coaching all the way down final
Missed radio calls, lost lookout [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Concise prompts only [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teaching landings mechanically
Unstable approaches when conditions change [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Teach for the approach actually flown [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Owning the lookout
A learner who enters maneuvers without clearing [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]
Correct it immediately; share the lookout [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Leaving the learner on the controls in a recovery
A fight for the controls [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Positive exchange; make sure the learner lets go [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Ignoring the learner's state
Distraction and errors from fatigue or outside stress [[25:28|AIH 1-24]] [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]
Ask, then switch to ground work, reschedule or end early [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]

check.q: Your learner can recite every PAVE item but never uses it unless you ask. Which instructor error does that point to, and what is the fix?
check.a: Teaching risk management as a separate subject. Integrate it into actual flight training and every preflight and postflight briefing [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

f1.caption: Figure 1-2. One of the most important decisions that the pilot in command makes is the go/no-go decision. Evaluating each of these risk elements can help the pilot decide whether a flight should be conducted or continued. (AIH 1-7)
f1.alt: A diagram titled Risk Elements with four boxes, Pilot, Aircraft, Environment and External Pressures, each with a short description, all feeding down into a box labeled Situation about keeping situational awareness of how they combine.

f2.caption: Figure 4-1. Risk Assessment Matrix. (RMH 4-2)
f2.alt: A grid with likelihood rows probable, occasional, remote and improbable, and severity columns catastrophic, critical, marginal and negligible. Probable-catastrophic, probable-critical and occasional-catastrophic are High; probable-marginal, occasional-critical and remote-catastrophic are Serious; most others are Medium; the negligible cells below probable are Low.

f3.caption: Figure 3-6. Example of a numerical FRAT. (RMH 3-10)
f3.alt: A risk assessment form with scored items under Sleep, How do you feel, Weather at termination, How is the day going, Is the flight day or night, and Planning, a total score box, and a scale from 0 to 30 marked Not complex flight, Exercise caution and Area of concern, running from Low risk to Endangerment.

f4.caption: Figure 9-8. During this procedure, a visual check is recommended to see that the other person actually has the flight controls. There should never be any doubt about who is flying the aircraft. (AIH 9-9)
f4.alt: Three stacked steps titled Positive Exchange of Flight Controls: the instructor says you have the flight controls, the learner answers I have the flight controls, and the instructor again says you have the flight controls.

f5.caption: Figure 1-14. Accidents often occur when flying task requirements exceed pilot capabilities. The difference between these two factors is called the margin of safety; in this idealized example it is minimal during the approach and landing. (AIH 1-26)
f5.alt: A 3D ribbon chart of task load over time through preflight, takeoff, cruise and approach and landing. A Pilot Capabilities band and a Task Requirements band rise and fall; the orange Margin of Safety between them shrinks almost to nothing at approach and landing.

f6.caption: Figure 2-1. The percentage of aviation accidents as they relate to the different phases of flight. The greatest percentage of accidents take place during a minor percentage of the total flight. (PHAK 2-2)
f6.alt: A bar chart of general aviation accidents by phase: preflight and taxi 3.5 percent, takeoff and initial climb 23.4, climb 3.3, cruise 15.7, descent 2.6, maneuvering 13, approach 9.7, landing 24.1 and other 4.7. Shaded bands show takeoff is about 2 percent of flight time, climb through descent about 83 percent, and maneuvering through landing about 15 percent.

f7.caption: Figure 1-12. Learners in training can be asked to identify hazardous attitudes and the corresponding antidotes when presented with flight scenarios. (AIH 1-23)
f7.alt: A two-column table telling the story of Steve buzzing a park. Macho: taking chances is foolish. Anti-authority: follow the rules, they are usually right. Invulnerability: it could happen to me. Impulsivity: not so fast, think first. Resignation: I am not helpless, I can make a difference.

scenario.title: Saturday stalls with a rushed learner
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Dana, a pre-solo learner with 14 hours, is booked for stalls and then pattern work in a two-seat trainer. It is a hot, hazy summer day with a ceiling of 2,800 feet broken over a busy practice area. Dana arrives late, says she had an argument with her boss and has to pick up her kids in two hours. The school's discrepancy sheet for the airplane has an open entry you have not read yet. On the last lesson you talked her through every second of final approach and she missed two tower calls.

questions.q: Run PAVE on this lesson. What hazards stand out?
questions.a: Pilot: Dana's emotional state and stress; the learner is also generally less proficient than you [[25:190|AIH 10-6]] [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Aircraft: the open discrepancy and limited performance or fuel load in a two-seat trainer on a hot day [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Environment: haze in a crowded practice area and a ceiling too low for stall practice [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. External pressure: her time limit [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: What do you do about the discrepancy sheet?
questions.a: Determine the official airworthiness status before preflight, read the current discrepancy report, resolve questions with maintenance and involve Dana in the process [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: Should you fly the stalls today? What are the options?
questions.a: Stalls below a cloud layer leave no room to recover and are a hazard you would create [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Coach Dana to name the risks (inadvertent IMC, too little altitude) and choose: stay in the traffic pattern, use a simulator or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: How do you handle her time pressure and the argument?
questions.a: Ease her schedule concerns and offer to reschedule, move to classroom work, or end early if she seems worried about time [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. Emotion is part of IMSAFE, and emotional upset decreases alertness [[25:12|AIH 1-8]].

questions.q: If you fly pattern work, how do you change your coaching from last time?
questions.a: Do most of the teaching before calling the tower [[25:192|AIH 10-8]], and use only concise prompting on approach; excessive coaching on final causes missed radio calls and cuts your own lookout [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

questions.q: After the lesson, how do you assess her risk management?
questions.a: Collaborative assessment: her self-assessment first, then yours, then a comparison [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Grade SRM as Explain, Practice or Manage/Decide; pre-solo, the goal is a basic risk analysis on her own by first solo [[25:32|AIH 1-28]] [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

skills.do: ACS: "Use scenario-based training (SBT) to demonstrate, teach, and assess risk management and Aeronautical Decision-Making (ADM) skills in the context of a Task specified by the evaluator." The examiner names a Task (for example short-field landings) and you build a scenario around it: run PAVE, rate risks on the matrix, choose TEAM actions, give the learner real decisions, then debrief with an SRM grade.
skills.practice: Pick three Tasks and write a one-paragraph scenario for each with a destination, desired outcome, desired performance level and possible inflight changes [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Teach one to a friend and grade them Explain, Practice or Manage/Decide [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

skills.do: ACS: "Identify, assess, and mitigate risks commonly associated with flight instruction by maintaining: a. Awareness and oversight of the learner's actions, with timely and appropriate supervision, intervention, or mitigation as needed; b. Awareness of the learner's cognitive/physiological state, with timely action to mitigate anxiety, fatigue, or other obstruction to learning; c. Overall situational awareness of the aircraft's dynamic state, its position in space, and vigilance for unexpected events or changing circumstances that occur in the environment." The examiner watches you guard the controls, step in at the right moment, notice when your "learner" is overloaded, and keep the airplane safe.
skills.practice: Fly from the right seat with a safety pilot playing a learner who makes AFH-style errors. Practice letting the error develop only as far as your limits allow, then take over cleanly [[25:179|AIH 9-9]] [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Before each flight, say your PAVE analysis of the instruction out loud [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

skills.do: ACS: "Model and teach safety practices, including maintaining: a. Collision avoidance while simultaneously providing instruction; b. Avoidance of unnecessary distractions; c. Coordinated flight; d. Awareness of who is manipulating controls through positive exchange of flight controls; e. Continuous awareness of the aircraft's dynamic state and position in the NAS." The examiner sees you keep scanning while you talk, keep the flight deck sterile in critical phases, keep the ball centered, use the three-step exchange every time, and know where you are.
skills.practice: Record yourself teaching a steep turn from the right seat. Count how often you clear and scan while talking, and check every control exchange used all three steps [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Brief the exchange procedure in every preflight briefing [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

quiz.q: A pilot planning a January trip sees widespread icing forecast and buys an airline ticket instead. Which TEAM action is that?
options: Transfer
Eliminate
Accept
Mitigate
quiz.why: Getting an airline ticket transfers the risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

quiz.q: You spend a ground lesson on an accident where the pilot skipped a weather briefing, guessed his fuel, launched tired and ran low near storms. What does the AIH say the error chain teaches?
options: Accidents are usually a chain of events, and breaking one link usually changes the outcome
Accidents usually come from one bad decision, so find that single cause and avoid it
Once a chain of poor decisions starts the outcome is fixed, so only the go/no-go call matters
Pilot error means weak stick and rudder skill, so the fix is more maneuver practice
quiz.why: It is usually not a single decision that leads to an accident but a chain of events, the poor judgment chain or error chain. Breaking one link in the chain is all that is usually necessary to change the outcome, and discussing real accidents is the best way to illustrate it [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. In the AIH example, the pilot could have made decisions on numerous occasions that may have prevented the incident [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

quiz.q: The "P" in PAVE covers which two major sub-elements?
options: Passengers and their needs; and programming of the avionics
Planning and performance; and preflight preparation of the airplane
Qualification, currency and proficiency; and aeromedical factors
Pressure from schedules; and the pilot's preflight paperwork
quiz.why: The P has two sub-elements: qualification, currency and proficiency, and aeromedical hazards checked with IMSAFE. It applies to both learner and instructor [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

quiz.q: Why should numerical FRATs be used with caution?
options: They take too long to complete
The FAA does not allow numerical FRATs in flight training
A low score can still hide a single extreme hazard
They do not use numbers
quiz.why: A hazard may not be on the list, or there may be only one risk but an extreme one, so the score suggests "go" [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

quiz.q: By the first solo, what should the learner be able to do with risk management?
options: Complete a full FRAT for cross-country flights
Teach it to other learners
Nothing yet; it starts after solo
Conduct a basic risk management analysis
quiz.why: Pre-solo training is instructor-led, and by the first solo the learner should be able to conduct a basic risk management analysis [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

quiz.q: What does the CARE checklist stand for?
options: Check, Assess, Reduce, Evaluate
Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors
Capability, Aircraft, Risk exposure, Environmental factors
Clear, Announce, Recover, Exit
quiz.why: Pilots process hazards with CARE: Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

quiz.q: After recognizing a thought as hazardous, what should the pilot do next?
options: Hand the controls to ATC
Ignore it until after landing, then discuss it in the debrief
Label it as hazardous, then state the antidote
Complete a numerical FRAT
quiz.why: Recognition is the first step; then label the thought as hazardous and state the corresponding antidote [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

quiz.q: Which obstacle to situational awareness does the AIH say is harder to recognize than fatigue?
options: Airsickness
Hypoxia
Spatial disorientation
Complacency
quiz.why: Complacency is harder to recognize because everything seems to be going smoothly [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

quiz.q: Your learner now has 30 hours and solid PAVE habits. What does the AIH say about who should lead the risk management discussions in your briefings?
options: You should always lead them, so nothing important is ever left out
Hold them only in the postflight debrief so the preflight stays short
Encourage her to take part and even lead them as her experience grows
Drop them from the briefings once her PAVE habits are solid
quiz.why: Risk management activity and discussion should be included in all preflight and postflight briefings, and learners should be encouraged to participate and even lead such discussions as their experience increases [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

quiz.q: The AIH says a few hazards are unique to flight instruction. Which is one of its examples of mitigating them?
options: Let the learner try new maneuvers before any training, so you see natural reactions
Choose practice areas with safe options, and fly maneuvers with enough altitude
Keep your hands well clear of the controls so the learner owns every outcome
Practice maneuvers low, where ground references make errors easier to see
quiz.why: The risk management techniques are the same as those taught to learners, but a few hazards are unique to flight instruction. The AIH's examples: ask the learner to fly specific maneuvers after giving appropriate training, choose practice locations that provide safe options, perform maneuvers with sufficient altitude, stay alert for the unexpected and be prepared to take over the controls [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: A learner rates a hazard as "remote" likelihood with "catastrophic" severity. What composite risk does the matrix give, and what does it imply?
options: Serious; no-go unless mitigated to medium or low
Medium; go, but mitigate if possible
Low; go
High; always cancel
final_quiz.why: Remote and catastrophic is serious (yellow), which implies no-go unless a new assessment after mitigation shows medium or low [[30:35|RMH 4-2]] [[30:36|RMH 4-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner cannot decide whether encountering IMC is "occasional" or "probable." What should you teach?
options: Skip that hazard
Average the two
Pick the lower one, to avoid cancelling too many good flights
Use the more conservative one, which places the risk higher
final_quiz.why: When unsure between adjacent values, apply the more conservative one and ask an instructor or more experienced pilot [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot keeps choosing likelihood values that make the matrix show green because he wants to get home. What matrix error is this?
options: Skewing
Exposure
Obsolescence
Accuracy
final_quiz.why: Using inputs that push the risk lower because of a desire to complete the flight is skewing [[30:35|RMH 4-2]].

final_quiz.q: A flight review pilot who flies only between rural Class E airports says he will soon fly regularly into Class B. What does the AIH say to add?
options: Mode C and ADS-B requirements and Class B environmental risks
Nothing; a flight review covers only the flying he does now, not future plans
An instrument rating, which is required before any flight into Class B
A full numerical FRAT for every local flight
final_quiz.why: If the pilot plans to change his operating profile, address the new risk management issues, such as Mode C, ADS-B and Class B environmental risk factors [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

final_quiz.q: An airline first officer asks you for a checkout in her own single-engine airplane. What risk management point does the AIH stress?
options: She can skip risk management in the checkout because airline CRM training already covers it
She may not be used to flying single-pilot without her employer's support
Professional pilots must complete a numerical FRAT before every personal flight
TEM replaces PAVE for her
final_quiz.why: Pilots who fly as a crew may not be used to flying single-pilot without the employer's support infrastructure; emphasize risk management in the training [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

final_quiz.q: A learner keeps calling off lessons for weather even though briefings show good conditions. The next lesson is stalls. What might be happening, and what helps?
options: Anti-authority; remind him firmly that the rules and the syllabus come first
Complacency; add distractions so the lessons challenge him again
Get-there-itis; have him set stricter personal minimums for weather
Worry about the stall lesson; explain it in more detail and encourage him
final_quiz.why: Repeated no-fly decisions in good weather may come from worry about stalls, landings or solo; more explanation and encouragement may ease the stress [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

final_quiz.q: You set up a soft-field takeoff. While the learner holds the airplane in ground effect it begins drifting toward the runway edge. What is your job?
options: Let the drift continue to the runway edge so she learns to correct it
Tell her to climb steeply out of ground effect to stop the drift
Talk her through the theory of ground effect
Keep drift within her control while watching pitch and airspeed
final_quiz.why: On soft-field takeoffs, monitor drift in ground effect, do not let it escalate beyond the learner's control, and watch pitch attitude and airspeed [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: The lesson plan calls for stalls, but today the ceiling is below the value you and your learner set for stall practice, so you drop the stalls. Which TEAM action is that?
options: Eliminate
Accept
Transfer
Mitigate
final_quiz.why: The AIH gives not practicing stalls when the ceiling is below a set value as an example of eliminating the risk [[25:187|AIH 10-3]].

final_quiz.q: As fatigue progresses, what sequence of errors does the AIH describe?
options: Commission, then omission, then microsleeps
Omission, then commission, then microsleeps
Microsleeps first, then errors
Only slower reaction times
final_quiz.why: Fatigue brings more errors of omission, then errors of commission, then microsleeps [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

final_quiz.q: In the AIH's Mooney accident analysis, the pilot flew into IMC knowing his vacuum pump had failed. What overall risk does the AIH read from the matrix?
options: Serious, because loss of control in IMC was catastrophic but only remote
High, since loss of control in IMC was catastrophic and at least occasional
Medium, because the pilot knew about the failure before entering IMC
Low, because the remaining instruments and the turn coordinator still worked
final_quiz.why: Catastrophic severity with occasional or probable likelihood gives a high (red) risk that needed mitigation; diverting to land in VMC may have been the best choice [[25:186|AIH 10-2]].

final_quiz.q: Which statement best describes when to use a full FRAT instead of a quick PAVE review?
options: Every flight, without exception, including a short local flight on a calm day
Never; FRATs are for airlines only
Only after an accident
For longer or complex flights; a short PAVE review suits a local flight
final_quiz.why: Scale risk management to the flight: abbreviated PAVE for a local flight, a FRAT for longer or complex ones [[25:189|AIH 10-5]].

final_quiz.q: A learner on a 180 degree power-off accuracy approach can tell you not to trade a stable approach for accuracy. What should you still expect?
options: Nothing; once she can state the rule, she will reliably apply it
She will always go around rather than accept an unstable approach
She may not be ready to apply it yet, so anticipate landing errors
She will land long every time until she masters the power-off glide
final_quiz.why: Learners may understand the rule but not be ready to apply it, so the instructor should anticipate potential landing errors [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot reads a NOTAM and hears the ATIS saying the runway closure has moved to the other parallel, yet he sets up for the runway that used to be open and is now closed. What is this?
options: Skewing
Resignation
Expectation bias
Scud running
final_quiz.why: Perceiving the information as it used to be, despite evidence, is expectation bias, and the RMH gives this exact parallel-runway example [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

takeaways: Teach identify, assess, mitigate in that order: PAVE to find hazards, the matrix to rate them, TEAM to act.
Start risk management on the ground before the first flight and put it in every briefing and debrief.
Use FRATs, but never trust a low score over one extreme hazard.
Build up by phase: you lead pre-solo, the learner leads by cross-country, and it never stops at recurrent training.
Instruction adds its own hazards; run PAVE on the lesson itself and keep enough altitude and space to take over.
Teach takeoffs on the ground, prompt concisely on final, and never teach landings by rote.
Model what you teach: lookout while talking, a sterile flight deck, coordinated flight and the three-step control exchange.
cfi_notes: The AIH 1-1 introduction says the tools for teaching risk management are in "Chapter 9, Techniques of Flight Instruction" [[25:5|AIH 1-1]]. In this edition Chapter 9 does exist under that name (positive exchange of controls, see and avoid), but the risk management teaching guidance is in Chapter 10, Teaching Practical Risk Management during Flight Instruction [[25:185|AIH 10-1]].

The sources give FRAT three names: Flight Risk Awareness Tool [[25:8|AIH 1-4]], Flight Risk Analysis Tool [[25:14|AIH 1-10]] and Flight Risk Assessment Tool [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]. The ACS uses Assessment; use that word on the checkride.

The anti-authority antidote reads "They are usually right" in the AIH and PHAK [[25:27|AIH 1-23]] [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]] but "They help prevent accidents" in the RMH [[30:21|RMH 3-3]]. Either is acceptable; know both.

The AIH defines situational awareness with four fundamental risk elements (the PAVE four) [[25:17|AIH 1-13]], while the PHAK lists five: flight, pilot, aircraft, environment and type of operation [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

The PHAK says about 80 percent of accidents are human factors related on one page [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]] and more than 70 percent on another [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]] [[1:50|PHAK 2-11]]. Quote the 80 percent figure with its source.

The AIH SRM grades list Explain, Practice, Manage/Decide and Not Observed, yet the same page uses "describe" as the first step of progressive grading [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. Describe is a maneuver grade in Chapter 6 [[25:137|AIH 6-6]]; be clear which rubric you mean.

The AIH chapter 1 says medium and low risks do not normally require mitigation [[25:8|AIH 1-4]], while chapter 10 and the RMH say medium risks should still be mitigated if possible [[25:187|AIH 10-3]] [[30:35|RMH 4-2]]. Teach the second: accept no unnecessary risk.
Learner-pilot words help you: when a learner says it will "probably" be okay, the PHAK says it is time for a reality check [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]]. Listen for it in preflight discussions.
Make a habit of letting the learner make the weather call on each flight while you keep the final choice [[25:32|AIH 1-28]]. It turns every lesson into risk management practice at no extra cost.
gaps: No source gives a minimum altitude or cloud clearance for teaching stalls or other maneuvers; the AIH says only "sufficient altitude" [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. Use the POH/AFM, your school's SOP and your own personal minimums.

The numerical FRAT example does not say which band a score of exactly 10 or 20 falls in, or whether several Planning items can be scored together [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]. Each FRAT sets its own thresholds [[25:15|AIH 1-11]].

The AIH says to brief the control exchange before flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]] but gives no standard words for an emergency takeover beyond "I have the flight controls" [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Agree on it in the briefing.

The sources do not give a method for deciding how far to let a learner's error develop; they say only to leave time and space to take over before it exceeds your ability [[25:190|AIH 10-6]]. That is CFI judgment.
The personal minimums adjustment table is called only a starting point [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]; the sources give no validated values for learners.

activities.title: PAVE the lesson
activities.intro: Tap each instruction hazard, then tap its PAVE bucket.

items.t: The instructor has never flown this glass-panel avionics suite
The learner shows up with a head cold
An overdue inspection the instructor does not know about
A two-seat trainer that must carry less fuel to take both of you
Haze over a crowded practice area
Practice approaches with no ATC surveillance
The learner must be back at work in an hour
Family worries about the cost of training

activities.title: Score it and set the limits
activities.intro: Use the RMH numerical FRAT (Figure 3-6) and the RMH personal minimums examples. Type your answer.

items.q: Score these FRAT items: did not sleep well (2), feel a bit off (2), destination at least 3 miles and 1,000 feet but under 3,000 and 5 (3), day flight (1), one thing after another (3), rush to get off ground (3), weight and balance verified (0), performance not evaluated (3), passengers briefed (0), computer program for all planning: no (0). What is the total?
items.why: 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 3 + 3 + 0 + 3 + 0 + 0 = 17, which falls in the Exercise caution range between 10 and 20 [[30:28|RMH 3-10]].

items.q: Same flight after mitigation: slept well (0), feel great (0), destination over 5 miles and 3,000 feet (1), day (1), great day (0), no hurry (1), weight and balance yes (0), performance yes (0), passengers briefed (0), computer program: no (0). Total?
items.why: 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 3, in the Not complex flight range below 10 [[30:28|RMH 3-10]]. Still check each hazard; a low score can hide one extreme risk [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

items.q: A pilot's baseline day VFR ceiling minimum is 2,500 feet. Today she is fatigued. Using the RMH adjustment for pilot factors, what is the lowest ceiling she should accept?
items.why: Baseline 2,500 ft [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] plus at least 500 ft for illness, medication, stress or fatigue [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]: 2,500 + 500 = 3,000 ft.

items.q: The same pilot's single-engine crosswind minimum is 7 knots. Passengers are pushing her to make a meeting. What crosswind limit does the RMH adjustment give?
items.why: Baseline 7 knots [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] minus at least 5 knots for external pressures [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]: 7 - 5 = 2 knots.

items.q: Tricia's calculated takeoff distance at 2,500 pounds is 3,600 feet over a 50-foot obstacle, and her personal minimum adds 20 percent. What runway length does she want?
items.why: 3,600 x 1.20 = 4,320 ft [[30:32|RMH 3-14]]. At gross weight the same margin on 4,700 ft gives 5,640 ft, longer than the 5,000-foot runway [[30:36|RMH 4-3]].

items.q: Tricia's airplane: empty 1,903 lb, max gross 2,740 lb. People 130 + 340 lb, baggage 120 lb, flight bag and gear 7 lb. Fuel weighs 6 lb per gallon. How many gallons can she carry?
items.why: 2,740 - 1,903 = 837 lb useful load; 837 - 130 - 340 - 120 - 7 = 240 lb; 240 / 6 = 40 gallons [[30:41|RMH 5-3]]. The 6 lb per gallon comes from 25 gallons = 150 lb [[30:31|RMH 3-13]].

activities.title: True or false: takeoffs and landings
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Excessive teaching on final approach can cause missed radio calls from ATC or traffic.
cards.why: True. Excessive coaching on final may cause missed transmissions [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

cards.s: Aiming and touchdown points are best taught as one fixed rule for every landing.
cards.why: False. The choice should not be mechanical; teach it for the aircraft, landing type, conditions and expected performance [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

cards.s: Before entering runway space, the instructor makes sure there is enough spacing from landing and departing aircraft.
cards.why: True. It avoids wake turbulence and spacing hazards and teaches sound decisions [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

cards.s: For an obstacle takeoff scenario, the instructor can name an imaginary obstacle at a realistic point.
cards.why: True. Scenarios should mimic real takeoffs without pushing an unsafe climb rate or pitch [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

cards.s: In strong winds the instructor can rely on the learner's skill alone.
cards.why: False. The instructor should have the skill to deal with the wind conditions [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

cards.s: Slower approach speeds on some short-field landings can reduce safety margins.
cards.why: True. Be aware of risks from slow flight or anything that reduces safety margins [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

activities.title: A lesson, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are the CFI for Riley, a pre-solo learner with 12 hours. Today's plan is slow flight, stalls and then landings.

steps.s: On the phone the night before, Riley mentions he has been sick. In the morning he says he feels "mostly fine."
options: Fly as planned; he said he is fine
Run IMSAFE with him and reschedule or switch to ground work if he is not well
Fly but skip stalls
Let him decide alone without discussing it
steps.why: Illness is the first IMSAFE item [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Build trust so learners disclose aeromedical issues early and can be rescheduled [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

steps.s: Riley is fine a week later. The ceiling is 2,500 feet broken and the practice area is hazy and busy.
options: Coach Riley to identify the risks, then change to pattern work, a simulator or reschedule
Climb through a gap and do stalls on top
Do stalls just below the clouds
Do the stalls but shorten them
steps.why: Coach the learner to identify risks such as inadvertent IMC and low altitude, then mitigate by changing the plan [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Teaching stalls below a cloud layer creates a hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: You choose pattern work. As Riley taxis onto the runway you remember you wanted to explain rotation speed.
options: Take the controls and demonstrate while explaining
Explain it now while he lines up
Keep quiet now; you should have taught it before the tower call, so give one short prompt at most
Ask tower for a delay and explain on the runway
steps.why: Do most teaching before contacting the tower; during the takeoff the learner may not hear or process it, and you risk missed calls [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

steps.s: In the pattern you are explaining the base turn when you notice Riley has not looked outside for traffic since takeoff.
options: Ask the tower to point out every airplane for him
Keep explaining; you are watching for traffic yourself
Take the controls for the rest of the pattern
Pause the explanation, have Riley scan and call out traffic, and remind him the lookout is shared
steps.why: If learners believe the instructor owns scanning and collision avoidance, they do not build constant vigilance, and a learner who skips the traffic check needs correcting right away [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. You and the learner are both responsible for the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

steps.s: Back on the ground you want to assess Riley's risk management, not just his landings. What do you ask about?
options: Only whether each landing met the ACS tolerances
His numerical FRAT total for the flight
Nothing; SRM is graded only on cross-country flights
How he reached his decisions, what resources he used and whether he assessed risk accurately
steps.why: In SRM assessment the AIH looks past technical accuracy: how did the learner arrive at a decision, what resources were used, and was risk assessed accurately on the go/no-go call [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
